transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Javier Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (BlueWave Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (BlueWave CTO), Emily Ng (Eng Manager), Raj Patel (SRE)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
- Customer is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted + private footprint; main concern is predictable unit economics for a conversational financial assistant and batch embed workloads.
- Discussed per-token pricing, batching and prefix/KV caching levers, quantization and model variants, Dedicated reserved pool economics vs Hosted.
- Agreed next steps: send pricing tiers, run a 48-hour benchmark on Dedicated with sample traffic, customer to provide anonymized logs, schedule pilot kickoff.

Topics seen: per-token math examples, effective cost per request, cache hit strategy for reused prompts, QPS and latency targets, SOC2/SAML and VPC concerns.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alicia Park: Hey everyone, thank you for joining — can you hear me ok?
[00:06] Priya Shah: Yeah, loud and clear. Thanks for scheduling, Alicia.
[00:08] Tom Reynolds: Thanks, Alicia. We only have about 50 minutes so we'd like to focus on cost and scale — sorry, economics per unit.
[00:15] Alicia Park: Totally, that's the plan — Marcus and Javier from SE will run through typical levers we see --- billing per token, batching, prefix/KV caching, model variants and dedicated sizing.
[00:25] Marcus Li: Quick context question — what's your primary workload mixture? Is it lots of short chat turns or long single-shot generation for docs?
[00:33] Priya Shah: Primarily chat assistant for customers: average session ~6 turns, average request payload is around 450 tokens in and 150 tokens out so about 600 tokens round trip. We also have nightly embedding jobs for personalization (~300M embeddings/month planned).
[00:49] Emily Ng: And our budget guidance from finance is roughly $20k per month for inference to start, with expansion if we can show predictable unit cost.
[00:58] Marcus Li: Great, that helps. Rough math example: if our hosted price is X per 1K tokens (we'll go into concrete numbers in a second), 600 tokens/request is 0.6 of a 1K token unit. But effective cost per user depends a lot on hit rates for caching and batching utilization.
[01:15] Tom Reynolds: Can you give us an example with numbers? We need to present something to the CFO.
[01:20] Alicia Park: Sure — high level first: hosted per-token base price for a Llama-2-ish open model might be $0.60 per 1K tokens for generation and $0.10 per 1K for embeddings — these are illustrative; we'll send exact tiers.
[01:33] Priya Shah: Ok that's helpful. But with 600 tokens/request how does that translate?
[01:37] Marcus Li: 600 tokens is 0.6 * $0.60 = $0.36 per request for generation before batching/caching or quantization. If you can get a 30% cache hit on repeated prompts (we often see template reuse in customer support dialogues), that's a 30% reduction on those requests. Batching for similar sequence lengths reduces GPU time per token — effectively you can cut cost per token by 10-30% depending on batching efficiency.
[01:59] Raj Patel: How do you measure cache hit rate? Are you doing prefix KV cache or just full-request caching?
[02:05] Marcus Li: We support both. Prefix/KV cache stores key-value states for the transformer cache so repeated initial prompts or system prompts can be skipped; full-response caching is also available for identical inputs. For chat, prefix cache is usually more valuable. Hit rate depends on your prompt engineering and frequency of repeated system messages.
[02:22] Priya Shah: We do standard system prompt plus user messages; about 40% of traffic includes the same system prompt, but user messages differ. So prefix cache might help on the first 100 tokens in many requests.
[02:34] Marcus Li: Exactly — that means you'd save the cost of the prefix tokens on each request. If the prefix is ~120 tokens, that is 20% of your 600 tokens. So 20% * $0.36 ~ $0.072 saved per request on the generation side, roughly.
[02:49] Tom Reynolds: And embeddings — you mentioned $0.10 per 1K. For 300M embeddings/month, what's the order of magnitude spend?
[02:56] Marcus Li: At $0.10 per 1K tokens, for embeddings usually they're billed per embedding unit, not token, but for rough numbers: 300M embeddings at say $0.0004 per embedding is $120k/month — but with reserved capacity and deduplication/caching that can drop. Also some customers do local embedding compute for high-volume offline batches.
[03:20] Priya Shah: That's above our starting budget; we'd need to see how dedicated or private options could lower unit cost for embeddings.
[03:26] Alicia Park: Yes, Dedicated pools with reserved capacity typically reduce per-token cost because you amortize GPU utilization. We can share a TCO model that compares Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private across your QPS and batch distributions.
[03:39] Tom Reynolds: Walk us through the Dedicated math — what drives the unit cost there?
[03:43] Javier Ramos: Sure — main drivers are GPU type (A100 vs H100 vs L4-like), how efficiently you pack requests into batches, KV cache hit rate, and model quantization. With reserved Dedicated capacity, you pay a committed monthly fee for a GPU pool. If you utilize it well (high sustained QPS and large batch sizes for offline embeds), unit cost goes down significantly compared to hosted spotty usage.
[04:05] Emily Ng: We're sensitive to latency — customers expect sub 400ms p95. Does Dedicated help with latency guarantees?
[04:11] Marcus Li: Dedicated lets you size your pool to hit latency SLOs; plus you can pin models and avoid noisy neighbors. Hosted is lower friction but no hard latency SLA on multi-tenant endpoints unless you move to a higher tier. We offer SLA-backed Dedicated for enterprise contracts.
[04:26] Raj Patel: For Private (VPC/on-prem) what are the major extra costs? Ops overhead and licensing?
[04:31] Alicia Park: Correct — Private includes a platform fee, support and potentially air-gapped packaging. You also factor in customer infra cost (network, GPUs, KMS, monitoring). For very regulated workloads the capex+opex can still be favorable if you need strict data residency.
[04:45] Tom Reynolds: Back to per-request math — what about quantization? If we move to 4-bit quantized weights how much do we save?
[04:51] Marcus Li: 4-bit quantization often reduces GPU memory footprint and allows higher batch sizes and lower memory bandwidth, which can reduce cost per token by 15-40% depending on model and workload. There is a small accuracy delta which you need to validate with your evals. We recommend running a QA/ROUGE-style regression on a sample set.
[05:10] Priya Shah: Could you do a quick hypothetical: if we take our 600-token request, 40% prefix cache of 120 tokens, batching yielding 20% improvement, and 4-bit = 25% reduction, what is the effective cost?
[05:22] Marcus Li: Stepwise: base $0.36 per request. Prefix cache 20% -> 0.36 * 0.8 = 0.288. Batching 20% -> 0.288 * 0.8 = 0.2304. Quantization 25% -> 0.2304 * 0.75 = $0.1728 per request. So about $0.17. At 50k requests/day that's ~$85k/month — so you'd need embeddings strategies or reserved capacity discounts to hit your $20k target.
[05:46] Tom Reynolds: That gap is alarming. Are there ways to reduce tokens per request?
[05:50] Priya Shah: We can reduce context length by summarizing earlier turns server-side, and move some logic from model to deterministic rules. But that affects quality.
[05:58] Alicia Park: Also progressive rollout: start hosted for low traffic to validate quality, then move embeddings/offline batch to dedicated, and only move chat to dedicated once you have stable usage for good amortization.
[06:09] Emily Ng: For the embeddings 300M number — that's a long-term projection. Could we do a hybrid where we embed in our data pipeline (airflow) on cheaper infra and keep chat on Redwood hosted?
[06:18] Marcus Li: Absolutely — many customers do nightly offline embedding pipelines on less expensive GPU infra and use Redwood for real-time chat. We can help model the split in the TCO sheet.
[06:26] Tom Reynolds: About benchmarking — what would you need from us to run a realistic Dedicated benchmark?
[06:31] Marcus Li: A representative sample of requests (payloads), distribution of sequence lengths, expected QPS ramp, and preferred model architectures. If you can share an anonymized log with timestamps and tokens per request, we can simulate prefix hit patterns and real-world batching.
[06:45] Priya Shah: We can anonymize and drop PII. We prefer S3 link with read-only and a short schema.
[06:50] Marcus Li: Perfect. Also, let us know your peak concurrent users and p95 latency target. We'll set up a 48-hour run on a Dedicated pool sized to your target throughput and deliver detailed token-level cost breakdowns and latency numbers.
[07:05] Tom Reynolds: What's typical variance between predicted and observed cost?
[07:09] Javier Ramos: If our simulation assumptions match your traffic patterns closely, we're often within 10-15% of observed. Mismatch mostly comes from different batching behavior in production vs synthetic load.
[07:21] Priya Shah: Would Redwood provide tooling for on-prem observability if we go Private? We need token-level cost and RBAC.
[07:29] Alicia Park: Yes — Redwood Console ships with token-level cost breakdown, route/model dashboards, tracing hooks, and RBAC, and we integrate with your SSO/SAML and KMS. For Private we can enable longer retention for logs as part of enterprise add-on.
[07:42] Raj Patel: Security questions — SOC2? Pen test? Encryption at rest?
[07:46] Alicia Park: We are SOC2 compliant; we can share the report under NDA. We support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Private, encryption in transit and at rest, and have a pen test history. We'll send the security pack.
[07:59] Tom Reynolds: Cool. On the pricing sheet — can you show both hosted price and a hypothetical dedicated model with a reserved monthly fee and per-token effective cost?
[08:07] Alicia Park: Yes, we'll provide a comparative TCO spreadsheet with sensitivity knobs: QPS, avg tokens, cache hit rate, batching efficiency, and discount tiers for reserved commits.
[08:17] Emily Ng: One more operational question: how hard is it to switch between model variants if we want to fall back to a smaller or quantized model for cost control?
[08:25] Marcus Li: We support model variants and can route by policy. You can define fallback chains: e.g., high-quality model for paid users, quantized smaller variant for anonymous traffic, and automatic fallback when Dedicated usage exceeds threshold. Switching is configurable in rollouts.
[08:38] Priya Shah: Can we get a sample rollback policy? We need to avoid regressions in fraud detection prompts.
[08:44] Javier Ramos: We'll share a canary+rollback playbook and point to examples in the console for A/B rollouts and auto-fallback settings.
[08:53] Tom Reynolds: Ok, let's talk discounting. At what commit level do you see meaningful per-token drops?
[08:58] Alicia Park: Commit tiers vary, but typical reserved contracts at enterprise scale reduce effective per-token costs by 30-60% depending on commit and utilization. We'll put mock numbers in the spreadsheet.
[09:09] Priya Shah: On the dedicated benchmark, can you emulate KV cache behavior? We have a lot of partial prompt reuse.
[09:15] Marcus Li: Yes, our benchmark harness can simulate prefix KV caches and per-session state to estimate hit rates. Provide sample turnover of conversation templates and we'll tune the simulation.
[09:25] Raj Patel: Networking wise, if we use Private VPC deployment, are there egress costs baked in?
[09:30] Alicia Park: Egress depends on your cloud/account setup; Redwood Private does not mark up egress but you'll incur normal cloud egress. We'll capture that as part of the TCO.
[09:39] Tom Reynolds: Let's get into an example billing line item set for a single day at 50k requests/day using the $0.17 effective cost you computed earlier.
[09:47] Emily Ng: 50k/day * $0.17 = $8.5k/day -> ~$255k/month, which is way above $20k, so we need to reduce tokens or move embedding work off-platform.
[09:58] Marcus Li: Correct — aggressive optimizations or re-architecting to reduce tokens per request is usually required to meet < $30k/month for chat at that scale. Another route: host only a portion of traffic on Redwood (premium users) and self-host cheaper baseline models.
[10:13] Priya Shah: Could Redwood run a hybrid where premium chat on Hosted and standard on Dedicated?
[10:18] Alicia Park: Yes, routing policies can split by user tier, region, or route. You can also do A/B between models to measure quality vs cost.
[10:26] Tom Reynolds: From a procurement perspective, what's typical contract length for Dedicated?
[10:30] Alicia Park: 12 or 36 month commitments are common; we also offer monthly burst options for early pilots.
[10:36] Marcus Li: For the 48-hour benchmark we propose to run on a small Dedicated pool sized to your peak QPS to surface batch and latency behavior. We'll deliver a CSV with token-level cost breakdown, average batch sizes, and cache hit metrics.
[10:49] Priya Shah: That will be useful. On model quantization regression testing — will Redwood help run evals?
[10:55] Javier Ramos: Yes, we have an eval harness and can run your prompt sets to show quality delta. We'll include simple metrics and examples.
[11:05] Tom Reynolds: Any gotchas for embedding deduplication? If we dedupe before embedding it reduces volume a lot.
[11:11] Marcus Li: Exactly — dedupe, vector store compression, and sharding embeddings into offline pipelines can cut your raw embedding units. Many customers pre-filter or chunk less.
[11:22] Emily Ng: We're also considering using a smaller embedding model for vectorization to save costs. Does Redwood support model mixing for embeddings?
[11:30] Marcus Li: Yes, route-based model selection is supported. You can use a smaller embedder for certain pipelines and a larger one for retrieval-critical flows.
[11:37] Priya Shah: Are there hidden fees for debugging or support during pilot?
[11:41] Alicia Park: During pilot standard support is included. For deep SRE integration or private on-prem installs there may be professional services which we'll quote separately.
[11:51] Tom Reynolds: Ok, on timeline — if you run the benchmark next week we can evaluate before EoM.
[11:56] Alicia Park: We'll aim to start benchmark by 2025-02-17 assuming logs arrive. Marcus to coordinate sizing.
[12:02] Marcus Li: I'll need an S3 link and expected peak QPS. Also, let us know any compliance blockers for sharing logs.
[12:09] Priya Shah: We'll scrub PII and share.
[12:12] Alicia Park: Anything else on cost levers we didn't touch?
[12:16] Raj Patel: One question — do you expose intermediate metrics so we can instrument cost per route in our app?
[12:21] Marcus Li: Yes, Console has token-level breakdown per route and per model, and you can export usage for internal chargeback.
[12:28] Tom Reynolds: Great. Let's try to keep the pilot narrow: start with chat for premium users only + nightly embedding offload; see numbers.
[12:35] Alicia Park: Sounds good. We'll follow up with the pricing sheet, TCO model, security pack, and benchmark plan.
[12:40] Emily Ng: Thanks, appreciate the pragmatic math.
[12:43] Priya Shah: Thanks all.
[12:45] Alicia Park: Thanks everyone — end notes: follow-up items in the action list. We'll send meeting notes and the expected artifacts.

End of transcript.
